versions.changelog:
Version 0.0.108 — updates that fail are caught, and uptime means something

An update is no longer treated as proven the moment it finishes starting. The
board now waits until the new version has been running for two minutes before it
stands down the rollback protection, so a version that starts cleanly and then
dies is still rolled back — which is the case the protection exists for. It also
refuses to stand down while an update is installed but not yet running, so the
protection is not spent on the version being replaced.

A board whose pixel driver firmware was left in the wrong place by an older
update now repairs itself at startup instead of refusing to start. That fault
could not be fixed by updating again, because the update that misplaced the
files was the one already installed.

Uptime is the daemon's own, everywhere it is reported. The status pages counted
from the first time anything asked rather than from startup, so a board running
for a week reported no uptime to whoever looked first — and the uptime announced
to other JBoards was the machine's, which does not change when the board's
software restarts. Both now report how long this board's software has actually
been running, which is what tells you whether it restarted.

Fleet updates verify what a board is running rather than what was copied onto
it, and send a restart request in the form the board accepts. Together these
made an update of another board report success while that board carried on
running its previous version.

Version 0.0.107 — rolling back to the previous version now works

Rolling back has never worked, in either form: the button on the Settings page
and the automatic restore that is supposed to undo a failed update. Restoring
the backup tried to write over the program that was running at that moment,
which the system refuses, and the failure was then reported as "no backup
available" — pointing at the one thing that was not wrong, while the backup sat
there intact. The restore now replaces the program the same way an update does,
and a failed rollback says what actually went wrong.

Rolling back also restores the pixel driver firmware, not just the program and
the web UI. A bad or misplaced driver payload is one of the likeliest reasons a
board would fail to start after an update, and restoring everything except that
would have left the board exactly as stuck as before.

Rolling back twice no longer loses track of the version. The restored version is
now read from the backup itself rather than inferred, so the board reports the
version it actually restored instead of "unknown".

Version 0.0.106 — updating no longer breaks the pixel output

An update installed its PRU firmware into the wrong directory. The package
carries the build layout, the board reads a slightly different one, and the OS
installer has always translated between them — the in-place updater did not. It
also cleared the whole firmware directory before copying, removing files the
package cannot put back. The board kept running normally because an update does
not restart the daemon, so nothing noticed until the next restart, at which
point the pixel driver could not find its firmware and the service failed to
start. Updating now places each file where the board expects it and only
replaces what the package actually supplies. This is the first release that has
been installed and then restarted end to end.

The firmware version shown around the UI was the build tag, not the version
installed. On a board that had ever been updated the two were different, so the
System page, the board identity other JBoards see on the network, the version
reported to FPP and xLights, the front-panel display and the stored system
configuration all kept naming the original factory build while the update card
correctly showed the installed one. They now all report the running version.

The update status also distinguishes what is installed from what is running.
Installing a package does not activate it — a restart does — and until now
nothing said so, which made an update whose restart never happened look
finished. The status now reports the running version alongside the installed one
and flags that a restart is pending.

Version 0.0.105 — the first update this board can actually find

Until now the device updater had nothing to check. It fetches a per-platform
manifest from the public distribution repo, but the release workflow only ever
attached a package to a GitHub release and never wrote that manifest, so every
update check failed. This release ships the missing publisher, and the manifest
now exists.

Integrity is checked against the manifest rather than against the package's own
metadata. A checksum stored inside an archive cannot attest to the archive that
contains it, which is why the in-package checksum field has always been empty
and the package's self-verification always passed. The manifest's SHA-256 lives
outside the artifact and is verified against the downloaded bytes before
anything is installed.

Also in this build:
- Streaming receive matches the ESP32 on every decode rule: preview-flagged
  E1.31 frames are never displayed, a terminating sender releases the outputs
  immediately, the DDP all-devices destination id is accepted, storage-flagged
  packets are not displayed, unsupported pixel formats are refused, and RGBW
  payloads pass through untouched so RGBW strips render correctly. The three
  protocol decoders are now literally the same code on both boards.
- DDP status and config queries are answered, so DDP-native discovery finds
  this board.
- Frame output waits for a complete frame instead of flipping mid-burst, so a
  slow multi-universe sender no longer shows half of one frame with half of the
  next.
- Pixel sources are arbitrated by priority rather than last-writer-wins: a
  running show is no longer stomped frame-by-frame by an effect or a sensor
  automation, and a source that stops writing stops owning the output.
- DMX channel mappings read from the correct source channels when universes are
  not 512 channels wide.
- Sunrise and sunset use the full NOAA solar algorithm, matching the ESP32
  minute for minute.
- Every thread the daemon runs now has a name, so `top -H` and crash reports
  are readable.
